title: "Continuous random variables"

The [discrete variable page](discrete-random-variables.qmd) treated separate, listable support values. Acoustic measurements such as vowel duration are different: between two possible durations lie indefinitely many others. How should probability be represented when modeled values fill an interval rather than occupy separate points?

We use Hillenbrand vowel durations to define a continuous variable, separate recorded precision from the model's continuous support, and then explain why intervals may have positive probability even though single points do not.

## Hillenbrand vowel duration

We use the vowel measurements from [Hillenbrand, Getty, Clark, and Wheeler (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872). The study recorded men, women, and children producing 12 American English vowels in /hVd/ words, measured duration and formant trajectories, and collected listener identifications. The [prepared teaching table](../data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv) is the audited `phonTools::h95` table from package version 0.2-2.2 under its BSD-2-Clause license; the [data record](../data/hillenbrand/README.md) documents the source and checksum.

One row is one vowel token nested within one speaker, and each speaker contributes one token for each vowel. The package imputed some F2 and F3 measurements, but our focal duration and F1 columns are complete. We restrict attention to adult men producing *heed* /i/, giving one token per speaker and avoiding a mixture over vowels.

The [canonical measurement dossier](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd#unit-and-observation-key)
defines the acoustic columns and observation key. Here `duration_ms` is the
elapsed vowel interval stored to whole milliseconds. The first displayed adult
male /i/ row is one concrete token: its speaker ID, duration, and F1 remain
linked rather than being three separate observations.

```{r}
#| label: load-hillenbrand-continuous
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
adult_i <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "man" & vowel == "i")

stopifnot(
  nrow(vowels) == 1668L,
  length(unique(vowels$speaker_id)) == 139L,
  all(table(vowels$speaker_id) == 12L),
  nrow(adult_i) == 45L,
  !anyDuplicated(adult_i$speaker_id),
  !anyNA(adult_i[c("duration_ms", "f1_hz")])
)

head(adult_i[c("speaker_id", "duration_ms", "f1_hz")])
```

Let $D$ map a token to its vowel duration in milliseconds. A useful modeled support is

$$
\operatorname{supp}(D)=(0,\infty)
$$

because durations are positive. This support is a modeling choice about the acoustic quantity, not a claim that the recording system stored infinitely precise values.

Positive real support is useful when the target is an underlying temporal
quantity: durations cannot be negative, and rounding can map many latent
durations to one stored integer. It is not forced by the file. Treating the
integers discretely instead would answer a question about recorded
millisecond values.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-duration-strip
#| fig-cap: "Raw durations for adult men producing /i/ in Hillenbrand et al. (1995). Small vertical jitter separates overlapping records."
set.seed(20261018) # dqr-allow: random-seed
ggplot(adult_i, aes(duration_ms, 0)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.035, width = 0),
    color = "grey"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Vowel duration (ms)", y = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

One tempting definition calls every variable with an uncountable range continuous. That definition is too weak for current purposes: an uncountable range does not guarantee that probability can be represented by a density. We use *continuous random variable* for the stronger, absolutely continuous case.

To see why range and distribution must be separated, start from one observed
token carrying a pair `(duration_ms, f1_hz)`. Now idealize such pairs as points
in a positive two-dimensional plane. Let

$$
\Omega\equiv\mathbb R_+^2
$$

and equip this space with its Borel sigma-algebra. Define the identity random vector

$$
X:\mathbb R_+^2\to\mathbb R_+^2,
\qquad
X(\omega)\equiv\omega.
$$

For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R_+^2$,

$$
X^{-1}(B)=B,
$$

so $X$ is measurable. This fact alone does not make its distribution absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity additionally requires the probability measure to admit a density with respect to two-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

A random variable $X$ is [**absolutely continuous**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Applied_Probability_%28Pfeiffer%29/07%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions/7.01%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions) when there is a nonnegative function $f_X$ such that

$$
\mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_A f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx
$$

for every measurable set $A$. We use *continuous random variable* for this class.

## A recorded value and a modeled point

The durations are stored as whole milliseconds. We derive the observed median and its empirical mass directly from the table.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-point-event
median_duration <- unname(quantile(adult_i$duration_ms, 0.5, type = 1))
recorded_mass_at_median <- mean(adult_i$duration_ms == median_duration)
continuous_point_probability <- 0 # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation

stopifnot(
  median_duration %in% adult_i$duration_ms,
  recorded_mass_at_median > 0,
  continuous_point_probability == 0
)

c(median_duration_ms = median_duration,
  empirical_mass_at_recorded_value = recorded_mass_at_median,
  continuous_model_point_probability = continuous_point_probability)
```

In the empirical distribution of the stored records, the value `r median_duration` ms has mass `r sprintf("%.3f", recorded_mass_at_median)`. Under an absolutely continuous model,

$$
\mathbb{P}(D=d)=0
$$

for every exact duration $d$, including the recorded median. This does not make a duration near $d$ impossible. An interval around it may have positive probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(d-\varepsilon<D<d+\varepsilon)>0.
$$

The distinction is between a stored, rounded measurement and a continuous model of the acoustic quantity. A spreadsheet column containing integers does not settle that representational choice.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does the empirical distribution assign positive mass to `median_duration` while an absolutely continuous model assigns point probability zero?
2. Give one reason to model the integer durations as rounded observations from a continuous process and one reason to analyze the recorded integers discretely.
3. Which dependence was removed by restricting to one vowel token per adult male speaker? Which population limitation remains?
4. Is a manually assigned five-point prominence score continuous? Explain from its response process rather than its display format.
5. A student says that whole-number storage proves duration is inherently
   discrete. Which two layers have been conflated?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The empirical distribution places mass $1/45=0.022222$ at the recorded median of 240 ms, whereas an absolutely continuous model assigns $\mathbb{P}(D=240)=0$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A continuous model can represent integer milliseconds as rounded measurements of latent duration, while a discrete analysis respects the actual recorded values without adding that measurement model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Selecting one /i/ token per adult male speaker removes repeated-speaker dependence within the subset, but the result remains limited to sampled adult men and the study's regional population. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A manually assigned five-point prominence score is discrete and ordinal because its response process offers only five ordered categories, regardless of numeric display. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The stored measurement resolution has been conflated with the model for the
   underlying acoustic quantity. Either a discrete recorded-value analysis or
   a rounded continuous measurement model may be appropriate.

</details>

The recorded whole-millisecond value and a positive continuous duration model
are different representations. So are measurability and absolute continuity:
the former does not imply the latter. The [next
page](probability-density-functions.qmd) represents continuous probability by
area across intervals.
